articles.title: Planning Application for Roof Replacement at Middleton Care Provider Refused
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has refused a care provider's application to replace the roof and alter the appearance of its offices in Middleton, citing concerns over the design's compatibility with the surrounding area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused a planning application from Vestacare, a care provider based at Unit 1 Westcroft Industrial Estate, 582 Manchester Old Road, Middleton. The application sought permission to replace the existing asbestos roof and external cladding, as well as to extend the shallow pitched roof of the building. The council's decision was based on the grounds that the proposed changes were "out of character" with the surrounding area.

In its design and access statement, Vestacare explained that the proposal aimed to refurbish and rationalise the existing industrial building. The company highlighted the need to remove aging asbestos cement roof sheeting and external cladding materials, and to install a new insulated roof and external wall cladding system. Vestacare argued that the existing roof forms were fragmented and visually inconsistent, and noted that several adjacent units within the estate had already undergone similar refurbishment works.

The care provider stated that the improved roof structure and increased internal clearance heights would facilitate a more efficient internal storage and distribution arrangement for its operations, which support adults with learning disabilities through day and supported-living services. The building serves as a central operational support and distribution facility for several care homes in the wider region.

The refusal of this application means that Vestacare will need to reconsider its plans for the building. The council's decision reflects ongoing concerns about maintaining the character of the industrial estate, which features a variety of commercial and industrial buildings of differing ages and appearances.

articles.title: Tram Services Disrupted in Rochdale This Weekend
articles.excerpt: Tram services between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre will be suspended on Saturday until 2pm, with additional service changes on Sunday due to maintenance work.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that no tram services will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre this Saturday, September 5, until 2pm. This disruption is part of ongoing maintenance work aimed at improving the tram network.

Additionally, on Sunday, September 6, from the start of service until 11am, there will be service changes across the network due to works at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar. Passengers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly during this time.

TfGM also reported that the lift at Derker tram stop is currently out of service. Passengers travelling towards Manchester can access the platform via a ramp from Cromford Street, while those heading towards Rochdale should use the track crossing for access. The lift at Failsworth is also out of service due to replacement works, and there is no step-free access available at this stop.

Customers requiring assistance or step-free access are encouraged to contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000 for journey planning support. Lines are open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and from 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

articles.title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing Appoints New Chair
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing reports significant progress in rehousing residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, with over 600 homes now vacant following safety concerns.
articles.content_html:
More than 600 homes are currently empty in Rochdale following the decision by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) to evict the remaining residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, officially known as College Bank. This decision was announced in October 2025 and has led to a significant reduction in the number of households living in the area, with only around 100 households still awaiting relocation out of approximately 760 total flats.

The eviction process, which was initially met with shock by residents, was clarified by RBH to take place over an 18-month period. As of late August 2026, 117 households have accepted offers for new accommodation, with 82 having already moved and a further 35 in the process of relocating. The remaining residents are primarily those who have not yet found suitable housing, as many have left due to what RBH describes as 'natural attrition', which includes reasons such as tenancy endings or voluntary departures.

The need for these evictions arose from safety concerns identified in a recent building survey. The survey highlighted various issues, including structural and electrical problems, water pumping system failures, roof damage, and rising costs for heating and lighting. RBH has stated that all tenants will receive support during their transition to new homes, including financial assistance for those affected. Leaseholders will have their properties purchased at market value.

This situation has been ongoing for nearly a decade, with plans for the demolition of some of the high-rises initially proposed in 2017. Although demolition was ruled out in 2023, RBH has since reopened discussions about the future of the tower blocks, stating that no final decision has been made regarding potential demolition. Local campaigners from the Save the Seven Sisters group have expressed concerns about the implications of these developments, fearing that the evictions may lead to a permanent loss of housing in the area.

articles.title: Middleton Library Hosts 'How to Research Your House' Event for Heritage Open Days
articles.excerpt: Middleton Library invites residents to explore the history of their homes through a special event aimed at uncovering local heritage and notable past inhabitants.
articles.content_html:
Middleton Library and Local Studies Centre is inviting residents to participate in a special event titled 'How to Research Your House' as part of the Heritage Open Days initiative. The event aims to equip householders with the skills and tools necessary to delve into the history of their homes, including information about former inhabitants and changes to the local area.

Participants will learn how to uncover fascinating details about their properties, which may include connections to notable figures such as architect Edgar Wood and writer Samuel Bamford. The event also encourages attendees to explore whether their homes have links to local celebrities like actress Gracie Fields or actor Don Estelle, who lived in College Bank.

The borough of Rochdale features a diverse range of homes, from modern constructions to traditional properties, including former mills and settlements dating back to the 12th century, such as St Chad’s and the area around Broadfield Park. This event presents an opportunity for residents to bring the history of their properties to life, whether they are interested in celebrated residents or the more obscure, potentially spooky histories of their homes.

The 'How to Research Your House' event at Middleton Library is a valuable resource for those looking to connect with their local heritage. For more information about the event and how to participate, residents are encouraged to visit the Middleton Library website or contact the library directly.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Signs Glenn Middleton on One-Year Contract
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC has announced the signing of winger Glenn Middleton from Doncaster Rovers on a one-year deal, alongside a loan for defender Charlie Tasker from Brighton.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC has confirmed the signing of winger Glenn Middleton from Doncaster Rovers on a one-year contract. The announcement was made on 1 September 2026, marking a significant addition to the League Two side's squad as they prepare for the upcoming season.

Glenn Middleton, 26, has a notable footballing background, having previously played for clubs including Rangers and Dundee United. He made 29 appearances for Rangers after joining from Norwich City in 2018 and spent three years at Tannadice before moving to Doncaster, where he played 35 matches in League One last season. Head coach Ian Watson expressed enthusiasm about Middleton's arrival, highlighting his pace and experience as key attributes that will benefit the team.

In addition to Middleton, Rochdale has also secured a loan deal for young defender Charlie Tasker from Brighton & Hove Albion. Tasker has captained Brighton's under-21 side in the Premier League 2, adding depth to Rochdale's defensive options as they look to strengthen their squad ahead of the new campaign.

The signings of Middleton and Tasker are expected to enhance Rochdale's performance in League Two, with both players bringing valuable experience and skill to the team. Fans will be eager to see how these new additions integrate into the squad as the season progresses.

articles.title: British Furniture Association Hosts Health and Safety Seminar in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The British Furniture Association, in partnership with Didac and Rochdale Occupational Health, will hold a health and safety seminar on 30 September, focusing on risks in the furniture industry.
articles.content_html:
The British Furniture Association (BFA) has announced a health and safety seminar titled 'Behind the Mask', which will take place at Rochdale Occupational Health (ROHS) on Wednesday, 30 September. This event is designed to address specific risks faced by workers in the furniture industry and is aimed at business owners, health and safety managers, and HR professionals responsible for workforce safety.

The seminar will feature expert-led presentations, live face-fit testing, and updates on relevant legislation. Attendees can expect workshops covering topics such as hearing and respiratory risks, stress in the workplace, and the importance of proper personal protective equipment (PPE). Phil Spademan, Managing Director of the BFA, emphasised the importance of providing meaningful training that is relevant to the industry.

Helen Yates, General Manager at ROHS, highlighted that events like this are crucial for empowering employers with the knowledge and tools necessary to protect their workforce effectively. The seminar aims to go beyond mere compliance with regulations, focusing on practical applications in the workplace.

The 'Behind the Mask' seminar is open to BFA members and clients of ROHS. Interested parties are encouraged to register in advance to secure their place at this informative event.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a well-loved part of Healey Dell’s landscape — a place of geology, industry and storytelling rather than documented supernatural events.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a well-loved part of Healey Dell’s landscape — a place of geology, industry and storytelling rather than documented supernatural events.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel is one of those local names that makes you slow your pace on the riverside path and look twice. The spot — a narrow gorge where the River Spodden squeezes through a cleft called the Thrutch — has been admired for centuries because the water-worn rock can take on shapes that, with a little imagination, suggest a pulpit, bench and alcove. The Dell itself is an established nature reserve and visitor attraction, with a heritage centre, tea rooms and family trails. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The most concrete, documented facts are straightforward. Healey Dell is managed and promoted as a nature reserve by the borough and its industrial archaeology — mill sites, lodges and a striking Victorian railway viaduct — is part of the site’s real history. The viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England (list entry 1317784). That history of mills and railways explains why the Dell became a popular Victorian beauty spot and why writers and guidebooks have long pointed to the peculiar rock features there. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The “Fairies’ Chapel” name and the other colourful stories attached to the Thrutch come from the region’s rich oral and printed tradition. The best-known version of the tale appears in John Roby’s 19th‑century collection Traditions of Lancashire, where Roby records romances about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, an enchanted chapel, the Fairy Queen and prophecies tied to Healey. These are literary‑folklore accounts: vivid, localised retellings that collectors like Roby shaped for Victorian readers. They are valuable as records of what people told and believed, but they are not documentary proof that supernatural events occurred. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Later local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre reprise Roby’s material and other regional legends — including stories that mix fairies, witches and a fairy king — and they explain the physical origin of the name: erosive action by the river produced a cavernous niche that looked church‑like to observers. The centre also records local floods and landscape changes (for example an extreme storm on 4 July 1838 that altered sections of the Spodden valley), which helps explain why the rock features seen by earlier visitors are not exactly the same today. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

What can we say with reasonable certainty, and what is pure folklore? Facts: the place‑name and rock feature are real; Healey Dell’s industrial remains and railway viaduct are documented and protected; the site has been a site of local tourism since Victorian times. Legends: the tales of a Fairy King turning witches to stone, of prophetic fairy queens or of Robin Hood connections are elements of local storytelling preserved in collections like Roby’s and in later retellings — entertaining and culturally important, but unsupported by independent historical evidence. If a claim cannot be verified in archival records or contemporary sources, it should be treated as folklore. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

If you visit Healey Dell today, bring two pairs of eyes: one for the geology, mill ruins and the listed viaduct that really are there; the other for the stories people have told around that landscape for 150‑plus years. The Fairies’ Chapel is best enjoyed as a meeting place of nature, industrial history and imagination — a reminder that some places are important precisely because they gather stories as well as stones. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Secures 3-0 Victory Against Shrewsbury Town
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's football team achieved a significant milestone by winning their first match since returning to the English Football League, defeating Shrewsbury Town 3-0 at the Crown Oil Arena on September 1, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Football Club celebrated a crucial victory on September 1, 2026, as they defeated Shrewsbury Town 3-0 at the Crown Oil Arena. This win marks the club's first success since their return to the English Football League (EFL) and the first three-point return under manager Ian Watson's tenure.

The scoring began in the 33rd minute when Baba Adeeko found the net, followed by Luke Hannant's impressive goal just ten minutes later, which saw him loft the ball over Shrewsbury goalkeeper Will Brook. The home side maintained their lead throughout the match, with goalkeeper Nils Ramming making a vital save to deny Will Boyle's header after the break. Substitute Jonny Smith capped off the performance with a goal in the 80th minute, sealing the victory for Rochdale.

In his post-match comments, Ian Watson expressed his satisfaction with the team's performance, stating, "I never get obsessed with the scoreboard... it was the way we played, the courage and bravery we showed, that was the most pleasing thing." He highlighted the importance of playing without fear and enjoying the game, noting that the players had previously been anxious on the pitch.

This victory not only boosts the team's morale but also sets a positive tone for their upcoming matches as they aim to build on this performance and establish a consistent winning mentality. Fans will be eager to see if Rochdale can maintain this momentum in their next fixtures.

articles.title: Mountain Rescue Team Finds Missing 71-Year-Old Man Near Piethorne Reservoir
articles.excerpt: A 71-year-old man with dementia was found by a mountain rescue team near Piethorne Reservoir after being reported missing on Saturday. The search involved police and a helicopter.
articles.content_html:
A mountain rescue team successfully located a 71-year-old man with dementia who had been reported missing near Piethorne Reservoir in Newhey on Saturday evening. The search operation was initiated after Greater Manchester Police received a report regarding the missing individual, prompting a coordinated effort that included the use of a police helicopter.

The Oldham Mountain Rescue Team was called in to assist with the search. According to a statement from the team, the man was equipped with an air tag that indicated he was in the vicinity of the reservoir. Initial searches conducted by police and the helicopter did not yield any results, leading to the involvement of the mountain rescue team.

The rescue team mobilised to the dam wall at Piethorne Reservoir, where their water section began searching the edges of the water both on foot and using a raft. Meanwhile, two additional search sections covered paths and tracks that had not yet been searched by police. Search dogs were also deployed to aid in the effort.

The missing man was found by a search dog and its handler before they reached their designated area. He was reported to be cold and confused but was safely located and returned to safety. This incident highlights the importance of community and emergency services working together in search and rescue operations.
